title: Piezo Channels and the Physics of Force

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: Which sensory functions principally depend on Piezo2?
cards.back: Touch and limb position (proprioception).
cards.quote: Piezo2 is a principal channel for touch and limb position:

cards.front: Why does increasing membrane tension favour opening a channel whose open state occupies more membrane area?
cards.back: Tension does work as the channel gains area, lowering the free energy of the open state relative to the closed state.
cards.quote: If a channel takes up more membrane area when it is open than when it is closed, membrane tension pushes it open.
cards.section: Three questions and one idea

cards.front: Silencing a candidate gene abolishes a cell’s mechanically evoked current. Does that establish that the protein forms the pore? Explain the inference.
cards.back: No. It establishes a requirement for the current in that cell; an accessory protein could also be required without lining the pore.
cards.quote: A protein required for a current could still be an accessory subunit of a channel made of something else.
cards.section: Which protein? A screen, and the claim it refused to make

cards.front: Introducing a candidate channel gene into another cultured cell confers a mechanically activated current. What does this establish, and what remains unresolved?
cards.back: Expression is sufficient to confer the current in that cellular setting. It does not establish that the introduced protein lines the pore.
cards.quote: The screen showed necessity in one cell line; expression showed sufficiency to confer a current in another.
cards.section: Which protein? A screen, and the claim it refused to make

cards.front: The decay of a mechanically activated current while the stimulus remains present is {{c1::inactivation}}.
cards.quote: Inactivation is the decay of a mechanically activated current while the stimulus is held;
cards.section: Which protein? A screen, and the claim it refused to make

cards.front: What type of conductance did ion-substitution experiments suggest for Piezo2’s mechanically activated current?
cards.back: A non-selective cation conductance.
cards.quote: Ion-substitution experiments pointed to a non-selective cation conductance for Piezo2, and its current inactivated quickly.
cards.section: Which protein? A screen, and the claim it refused to make

cards.front: How many transmembrane helices are in one mouse PIEZO2 protomer and in the complete trimer?
cards.back: 38 per protomer; 114 in the complete three-subunit channel.
cards.quote: holds 38 transmembrane helices per protomer, which means 114 in the trimer.
cards.section: Blades, beam and dome

cards.front: A membrane dome’s shadow on the flat plane of the surrounding membrane is its {{c1::projected area}}.
cards.quote: Its projected area is its shadow on the flat plane of the surrounding membrane: the area it occupies seen from above.
cards.section: Blades, beam and dome

cards.front: Model a PIEZO2 dome as a spherical cap with rim radius a = 14 nm and depth h = 10 nm. Surface area is π(a² + h²); projected area is πa². What projected area is gained on flattening without stretching?
cards.back: ΔA = π(a² + h²) − πa² = πh² = π(10 nm)² ≈ 314 nm², or about 310 nm². This is idealized geometry, not a measured opening area.
cards.quote: Flattened, all 930 nm² lies in the plane, so the projected area rises by about 930 − 616 ≈ 310 nm².
cards.section: Blades, beam and dome

cards.front: Two idealized spherical membrane caps have the same depth but different rim radii. If both flatten without stretching, which gains more projected area, and why?
cards.back: They gain the same projected area. For a spherical cap the gain is πh², so equal depths give equal gains regardless of rim radius.
cards.quote: It depends on how deep the dome is, not on how wide.
cards.section: Blades, beam and dome

cards.front: Membrane {{c1::tension}} is an in-plane stretch measured as force per unit length.
cards.quote: Membrane tension, T, is an in-plane stretch: force per unit length of membrane.
cards.section: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve

cards.front: In the two-state tension-gating model, what is the free energy of the open state relative to the closed state? Define the area term.
cards.back: ΔG = ΔG₀ − T·ΔA; ΔA is the increase in projected area on opening, and T is membrane tension.
cards.quote: So tension lowers the free energy of the open state relative to the closed one: ΔG = ΔG₀ − T × ΔA
cards.section: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve

cards.front: What physical preference does ΔG₀ represent in the two-state tension-gating model?
cards.back: The open-minus-closed free energy in a slack membrane; a positive value means the closed state is favoured without tension.
cards.quote: ΔG₀ is how strongly the channel prefers to be closed in a slack membrane.
cards.section: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve

cards.front: Why is the half-activation tension T50 = ΔG₀/ΔA in an equilibrium two-state channel model?
cards.back: At half activation, open and closed are equally favoured: ΔG = 0. Thus T50·ΔA = ΔG₀.
cards.quote: At T = T50 the exponent is zero, so ΔG is zero and half the channels are open.
cards.section: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve

cards.front: How does the slope factor k of an equilibrium two-state current–tension curve encode the opening area ΔA?
cards.back: k = k_B T_abs/ΔA, where k_B T_abs is thermal energy. A larger opening area gives a smaller k and a steeper curve.
cards.quote: The slope factor is thermal energy divided by that area. A larger area gives a smaller k and a steeper switch.
cards.section: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve

cards.front: A two-state channel’s resting closed-state preference ΔG₀ increases, while opening area and temperature stay fixed. What happens to T50 and k, and why?
cards.back: T50 increases while k stays unchanged. T50 = ΔG₀/ΔA depends on resting energy, whereas k = k_B T_abs/ΔA does not.
cards.quote: The half-activation tension is the channel's resting preference for closed, divided by the area it gains on opening.
cards.section: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve

cards.front: Two equilibrium two-state channels at the same temperature have the same T50, but one has a smaller k. What must differ about its opening area and resting energy?
cards.back: The smaller-k channel has a larger ΔA, by k = k_B T_abs/ΔA. Its ΔG₀ must also be larger in the same proportion, because T50 = ΔG₀/ΔA is unchanged.
cards.quote: With that assumption, matching the two forms gives each fitted number a physical meaning: T50 = ΔG₀ / ΔA.
cards.section: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve

cards.front: What must remain constant for a normalized channel current to track the fraction of available channels open?
cards.back: Conductance and channel availability must stay constant, and the plateau must correspond to the available channels being open.
cards.quote: constant conductance and availability, and a plateau where the available channels are open.
cards.section: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve

cards.front: A membrane tension of 1 pN/nm equals {{c1::1 mN/m}}.
cards.quote: 1 pN/nm and 1 mN/m are the same quantity.
cards.section: Tension pays for area: from an energy to a curve

cards.front: Why must patch curvature be measured before pressure can be used to compare membrane tension between spherical patches?
cards.back: Tension is T = R·|Δp|/2 for uniform tension. The same pressure difference gives different tensions when the radii of curvature differ.
cards.quote: with R the patch's radius of curvature: T = R × (pressure difference) / 2
cards.section: Reading a patch: from pressure to current, and back to an area

cards.front: A spherical membrane patch has uniform tension and a measured radius of curvature of 1.5 μm. A pressure difference of magnitude 4000 Pa is applied. Using T = R·|Δp|/2, calculate the tension in mN/m.
cards.quote: with R the patch's radius of curvature: T = R × (pressure difference) / 2
cards.section: Reading a patch: from pressure to current, and back to an area

cards.front: Two spherical patches have different current–pressure curves and different curvatures. How would you test whether geometry, rather than channel tension sensitivity, explains the difference?
cards.back: For uniform tension, measure curvature across the pressure range and convert each point using T = R·|Δp|/2. Compare normalized current–tension curves. Their overlap would support a geometry explanation, because pressure alone does not specify tension.
cards.quote: For a patch shaped like part of a sphere, with uniform tension, the Young–Laplace relation converts pressure into tension,
cards.section: Reading a patch: from pressure to current, and back to an area

cards.front: An illustrative mouse Piezo1 patch reaches T = 3.5 mN/m. Using central fit values T50 = 2.7 mN/m and k = 0.8 mN/m, calculate I/Imax = 1/[1 + exp((T50 − T)/k)].
cards.back: (T50 − T)/k = (2.7 − 3.5)/0.8 = −1. Thus I/Imax = 1/(1 + e⁻¹) ≈ 0.731, about 73% of the fitted plateau.
cards.quote: a half-activation tension T50 = 2.7 ± 0.1 mN/m and a Boltzmann slope factor k = 0.8 ± 0.1 mN/m.
cards.section: Worked problem: from patch pressure to predicted current, and back to an area

cards.front: An equilibrium two-state fit has k = 0.4 mN/m. At thermal energy k_B T_abs = 4.1 × 10⁻²¹ J, what effective opening area follows from ΔA = k_B T_abs/k? Use 1 nm² = 10⁻¹⁸ m².
cards.back: ΔA = (4.1 × 10⁻²¹ J)/(0.4 × 10⁻³ N/m) = 1.025 × 10⁻¹⁷ m² = 10.25 nm², about 10 nm². This is a model-derived effective area.
cards.quote: Run the fit backwards, reading it as a two-state switch:
cards.section: Worked problem: from patch pressure to predicted current, and back to an area

cards.front: Use fitted effective area ΔA = 5.1 × 10⁻¹⁸ m² and T50 = 2.7 mN/m to estimate ΔG₀ = T50·ΔA. Express it in joules and in thermal units of 4.1 × 10⁻²¹ J.
cards.back: ΔG₀ = (2.7 × 10⁻³)(5.1 × 10⁻¹⁸) = 1.377 × 10⁻²⁰ J ≈ 1.4 × 10⁻²⁰ J, or 3.36 ≈ 3.4 thermal units. It is derived from the fit, not independently measured.
cards.quote: it is computed from the fitted area, so it is not an independent measurement of how strongly the channel prefers closed.
cards.section: Worked problem: from patch pressure to predicted current, and back to an area

cards.front: In the mouse Piezo1 prepulse protocol, T50 fell from 2.2 to 1.4 mN/m. Why should the separate pressure-clamp value of 2.7 mN/m not be the baseline for that comparison?
cards.back: The values belong to different protocols. Compare 2.2 with 1.4 within the prepulse protocol; the apparent sensitivity depends on the channel’s preceding tension history.
cards.quote: Compare those two with each other, not with 2.7, which belongs to the other protocol.
cards.section: Worked problem: from patch pressure to predicted current, and back to an area

cards.front: If the entire structural expansion of 300 nm² were coupled to two-state Piezo1 opening, calculate k = k_B T_abs/ΔA at thermal energy 4.1 × 10⁻²¹ J. Compare with fitted k = 0.8 mN/m.
cards.back: k = (4.1 × 10⁻²¹)/(300 × 10⁻¹⁸) = 1.37 × 10⁻⁵ N/m ≈ 0.014 mN/m. The fitted factor is about 59 times larger (roughly sixty-fold), so the fitted switch is much shallower.
cards.quote: The half-activation tensions are of the same order (1.9 mN/m calculated from structure and a stiffness, 2.7 from a patch fit), but the slope factors differ about sixty-fold.
cards.section: The gap between structure and current

cards.front: Why does a structural comparison showing about 300 nm² of expansion not establish that Piezo1 gains that area on pore opening?
cards.back: The flattened structural class may not be the open channel. Even if flattening contributes to gating, only part of it may be coupled to the pore.
cards.quote: The flattened class may not be the open channel, which is the hedge Yang and colleagues make.
cards.section: The gap between structure and current

cards.front: A population current curve is shallower than individual channel curves. Under what specific assumptions does its slope-derived area underestimate the common opening area, and why?
cards.back: Assume independent equilibrium two-state switches with a common ΔA and differences only in T50. Threshold spread broadens the population curve, increasing fitted k; since ΔA = k_B T_abs/k, the inferred area falls. Outside those assumptions it is not a bound.
cards.quote: If the channels are independent two-state switches that differ only in T50, spread can only make the population curve shallower.
cards.section: The gap between structure and current

cards.front: In the membrane-footprint model of Piezo gating, why can membrane beyond the protein contribute to tension’s work?
cards.back: The surrounding bilayer bends into a skirt beyond the curved protein. Tension therefore does work on this membrane footprint as well as on the protein.
cards.quote: so tension does work on the footprint as well as on the protein.
cards.section: The gap between structure and current

cards.front: A purified mechanosensitive channel still opens in response to mechanical stimulation in an artificial lipid bilayer containing no other cellular components. What does this establish about gating requirements in that preparation?
cards.back: Protein plus lipid suffices for mechanical gating there; a cellular tether is not required in that preparation.
cards.quote: Because it opened, protein plus lipid is sufficient in that preparation, and no tether is required there.
cards.section: Lipid or tether?

cards.front: A purified channel is mechanically activated in lipid alone, yet disrupting a protein linker prevents mechanically evoked gating in intact cells. Can both results be valid? Explain using necessity and sufficiency.
cards.back: Yes. Protein plus lipid is sufficient in the bilayer, while the linker can be necessary for force delivery in the intact-cell preparation. Sufficiency in one setting does not exclude an additional route in another.
cards.quote: Bilayer sufficiency cannot exclude a second route in an intact cell,
cards.section: Lipid or tether?

cards.front: A tether pulls directly on a channel without changing membrane tension. Would the −T·ΔA term alone describe that added force input? What changes in the energy model, and why?
cards.back: An additional work term is needed: tether force times displacement. The −T·ΔA term accounts for work by membrane tension, not direct tether pulling.
cards.quote: it could pull on the channel directly, which would add its own work term, force times distance.
cards.section: Lipid or tether?

cards.front: Deleting a proposed force-transmission protein throughout development reduces adult sensory responses. What follow-up would better test its immediate mechanical role, and why?
cards.back: Disrupt the protein acutely in adult sensory cells and record before tissue architecture changes. The rule is to separate immediate function from developmental and structural effects of lifelong deletion.
cards.quote: A germline deletion of a cadherin or a catenin changes development, adhesion and skin structure,
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: After an acute perturbation, a skin stimulus evokes fewer sensory spikes. How could paired ending recordings and current–tension measurements distinguish altered force delivery from altered channel tension sensitivity?
cards.back: Compare spike responses with channel current across measured tensions. Preserved current–tension behaviour despite altered stimulus-to-spike responses supports changed force delivery. A changed current–tension curve suggests altered gating or availability; the rule is to measure the channel’s actual mechanical input.
cards.quote: a tether could change the mechanics of force delivery to the ending without changing the channel's tension sensitivity,
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Acute disruption of a proposed Piezo2 linker shifts the current–tension curve in a sensory ending. What controls are needed before assigning the shift to loss of a specific gating interaction?
cards.back: Check channel abundance, patch mechanics and tissue architecture, then rescue the interaction. The rule is that a linker can change local mechanics or availability; a shifted curve alone does not isolate direct gating.
cards.quote: A shifted curve alone is not decisive, because a linker can also alter local membrane mechanics or channel availability,
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In HEK293T recordings, which inactivation changes were shared by human PIEZO2 variants I802F and E2727del, and which occurred only with E2727del?
cards.back: Both recovered faster from inactivation; only E2727del slowed inactivation during a maintained pulse.
cards.quote: Both I802F and E2727del accelerated recovery from inactivation; only E2727del slowed inactivation during the pulse.
cards.section: Variants that change inactivation, and what people report

cards.front: Based on the two reported individuals with compound inactivating PIEZO2 variants, what would you predict about apparent limb-position impairment in trials without visual cues versus eyes-open trials, and why?
cards.back: More pronounced impairment is expected without visual cues. Eyes-open trials can conceal part of the proprioceptive deficit because vision helps compensate for impaired limb-position input.
cards.quote: had impaired discriminative touch and profound proprioceptive impairment that worsened without visual cues, while retaining other abilities.
cards.section: Variants that change inactivation, and what people report

cards.front: Why should the mouse Piezo2 deletion phenotype not be described as the observed human PIEZO2 loss-of-function phenotype?
cards.back: Adult mice with Piezo2 deleted from sensory neurons and Merkel cells showed almost complete light-touch loss. The two people had selective touch and profound proprioceptive deficits with residual abilities; the preparations and outcomes differ.
cards.quote: the human ones are selective deficits with residual abilities, and the two should not be merged.
cards.section: Variants that change inactivation, and what people report

cards.front: Why can the closed/open two-state tension model not explain PIEZO2 variant effects on inactivation or recovery?
cards.back: It contains no inactivated state. It therefore cannot represent entry into inactivation or recovery from it.
cards.quote: The two-state model has no inactivated state, so it covers neither inactivation nor recovery from it,
cards.section: Where the idea stops

cards.front: What channel mediated the dehydration following Yoda1-induced calcium entry in mouse red blood cells?
cards.back: The Gardos channel, a calcium-activated potassium channel.
cards.quote: Yoda1 produced calcium influx followed by dehydration that depended on the Gardos channel, a calcium-activated potassium channel.
cards.section: Piezo1 variants and red blood cells

cards.front: In mouse red blood cells, selectively block the Gardos channel while preserving the calcium influx induced by Yoda1. What happens to the reported dehydration, and why?
cards.back: The Gardos-dependent dehydration is prevented despite calcium entry. In this preparation, dehydration depends on the downstream Gardos channel, so calcium influx alone is insufficient.
cards.quote: Yoda1 produced calcium influx followed by dehydration that depended on the Gardos channel, a calcium-activated potassium channel.
cards.section: Piezo1 variants and red blood cells

cards.front: Which alternatively spliced exon conferred high Piezo2 tension sensitivity in the tested splice variants, and how broad is that conclusion?
cards.back: Exon 35. It is evidence from one recent study of tested variants, not a field-wide rule.
cards.quote: An alternatively spliced exon, exon 35, was enough to confer high tension sensitivity on Piezo2 in the tested splice variants
cards.section: Piezo2 tension sensitivity and splice variants

cards.front: What did the 2026 cell-derived-membrane study propose about force as a requirement for Piezo1 conduction?
cards.back: Force is necessary but not sufficient; lipid context also matters. This is a proposal from one recent study.
cards.quote: They propose that force is necessary but not sufficient.
cards.section: Piezo1 in cell-derived membranes
